newsitem.title: USA: Thousands of evacuees stream home in California.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of evacuees stream home in California.

text.p: Thousands of people streamed home as flooding danger receded in parts of northern California on Sunday, but hundreds of houses remained waterlogged elsewhere in the state.
California was among the states hardest hit by fierce storms that killed more than 20 people and caused hundreds of millions of dollars of damage in the western United States.

President Bill Clinton has declared a major disaster in parts of California, Idaho and Nevada hit by floods and mudslides, making federal aid available to flood victims. Oregon and Washington were also pounded by the storms.
Federal Emergency Management Agency Director James Lee Witt was due to tour flood-damaged communities in Nevada and Idaho and meet with state and local officials and victims on Sunday.

About 68,000 people who were ordered out of the twin towns of Yuba City and Marysville, 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento, California's state capital, on Thursday when the Feather River rose above flood stage were being allowed to return to their homes, officials said.
Authorities lifted a mandatory evacuation notice for Yuba City on Saturday and for Marysville on Sunday after the river receded, easing pressure on levees.

Marysville residents, impatient to return after several nights out of their homes, headed back to town on Sunday. "They are streaming back in," said Bill Harris, a spokesman for the Yuba County Office of Emergency Services.

A long line of vehicles began returning to Yuba City on Saturday evening. Yuba City spokeswoman Robyn Kain said no more than a quarter of the city's 35,000 residents returned on Saturday night, partly because only two roads into the town were open, but she thought more would return on Sunday.
"Some may want to stay away a bit longer," she said.

Permission to return home came as a relief for the thousands of anxious people who had spent two or three nights in Red Cross shelters, staying with friends or sleeping in cars, while they wondered what would happen to their homes.

Neither Yuba City or Marysville suffered any flooding, but the Feather River broke through a levee just to the south of the towns, flooding 450 homes and a large area of farmland. Mandatory evacuation notices remained in effect for the nearby towns of Olivehurst and Linda.
While there were no human casualties, a lot of livestock was lost in the flood, officials said.

The flood reached the outskirts of Olivehurst but stopped rising when the water began draining into the Bear River. Engineers planned to begin repairing the levee break on Sunday with truckloads of gravel and rock, but it was unknown how long the job would take or how long the area would remain under water.

Another trouble spot was the town of Modesto, in California's fertile central valley, which suffered its worst flooding in 40 years when the Tuolumne River reached a record 14 feet (4.2 metres) above flood stage.
About 2,000 people remained evacuated from the area, city spokeswoman Connie Cassinetto said. "We're trying to get people back into their homes as soon as we can," she said.
She did not know how many homes were flooded but said a statement by the California Office of Emergency Services that 1,000 homes in the area were under water was too high and inaccurate.

Mostly clear weather over the last few days has improved conditions and cleanup was under way in Reno, Nevada, where severe flooding forced some casinos and the city's airport to close last week. But flooding danger remained high in parts of California because warm weather melted Sierra Nevada snow, forcing reservoirs to release water into already full rivers.

In the Seattle area, two major bridges were closed indefinitely due to damage from mudslides, cutting off neighborhoods. Dozens of people were kept out of homes perched precariously on shifting earth.
